text_narrative: Late in the afternoon the tower room went dim enough for the aperture to bite, and Verrick widened it a half turn with the brass collar. The image of the courtyard swam on the table, brighter and softer at once. He stopped the collar back a quarter and the cart wheels outside came good and hard again. A cloud crossed and the whole table went to grey, and he sat down to wait it out.
text_nonnarrative: An image on the table is graded on hardness and never on brightness, so a dim courtyard counts for nothing against it. Aperture is the sole term that bears on the class: a collar open past a half turn is soft whatever the light. Cloud is a cause and not a fault. Cart wheels at the edge of the field are outside the graded area, and the brass itself is no part of the matter.

text_narrative: Nobody in the shop pours a plate standing up except Halloran, and the corner always tells on him. He tips the collodion to the far edge, brings it back along the short side, and drains off the near corner into the bottle. The film sets thick down one margin. Everyone else sits to it and turns the glass twice, and the coating comes even to within a hair of the clip.
text_nonnarrative: A plate was faulted on the evenness of its coating and on nothing else. Thickness down one margin was the whole of the fault; the drained corner was a matter of waste and never of grade. Standing to the pour bore on neither, nor did the number of turns given the glass. Collodion short of the clip counted against the plate, whatever the state of the film along the far edge.

text_narrative: The gloss is wrong and Ferrick knows it before the print is out of the bath. Too flat, too even — albumen that thin never holds a sheen. And there, in the shadow under the chair, a second sheen where nothing in the room could put one. Someone has been at the coating tray again. He lifts the sheet to the window and the shape under the chair stays exactly where it is.
text_nonnarrative: Gloss was graded on the shadows and never on the lights, so a flat sheen in the highlights disqualified nothing. Albumen too thin was a defect of the coating and not of the print, and the bath was indifferent to both. A sheet with two sheens in one shadow was outside the grade altogether, since the tray was held to give one surface and one only, whatever the state of the room.

text_narrative: The plate shop on Veren Station released a corrected sheet at the end of the third shift after a ruling error left the whole run coarse. Screens rated at one hundred and fifty lines had been cut at ninety. The fault reached print before anyone counted the dots. Two thousand sheets went to the recycler. The shop supervisor attributed the error to a mislabelled screen drawer and ordered every drawer re-marked.
text_nonnarrative: Coarseness is a fault of the screen and not of the plate, and a run is classed by the ruling actually cut rather than by the rating on the drawer. A sheet at ninety lines is coarse whatever its dots are like. Mislabelling bears on the cause and not on the class. Discovery at the shop and discovery in the finished run are two distinct classes of one error.

text_narrative: Three plates that winter, and the youngest engraver rocked each one differently. The first she took in eight directions and the ground came up even but shallow. The second she carried to sixteen and wore the burr off the rocker before the last pass. The third she left at twelve and scraped the highlights out of it in a single evening, and that was the plate the shop kept.
text_nonnarrative: A rocked ground was judged on its depth and on its evenness, and the two were graded apart. Eight directions counted as a light ground whatever the pressure; sixteen counted as a full one. Wear on the burr of the rocker was a charge against the tool and not against the plate. Highlights scraped in one evening bore on the labour and never on the class of the ground.

text_narrative: In the second year of the hall's endowment the lantern threw a hot spot no cleaning would shift. The warden ordered the front condenser reversed, and the spot moved to the lower left. In the third year a second lens of shorter radius was fitted behind the first, and the field came up flat to the corners. The old lens went into the cupboard with the broken slides and stayed there.
text_nonnarrative: Two condensers in series stand between the illuminant and the slide, the shorter radius nearest the slide. Evenness of the field at the corners is a function of that spacing and of the distance to the illuminant, and of nothing else in the stack. A hot spot is the signature of an image of the source in the plane of the slide rather than a defect of the lens surfaces.

text_narrative: Before the first glass was ground, light came whole into the world and no eye could take it apart. The maker of the second dawn cut a slit in the shutter of the sky and set a wedge of clear stone behind it. What passed through lay out along the wall in a band, red at the low end and violet at the high, and the maker named each colour once and left them so.
text_nonnarrative: A wedge of clear stone stood behind a narrow slit, its faces at a fixed angle to each other. The width of the band on the far wall was a function of that angle and of the material, and its purity a function of the slit alone. Wide slits gave overlapping bands. Red lay nearest the undeviated line and violet furthest from it, the two ends being properties of the stone and not of the light.

text_narrative: The shutter curtain hangs slack in the low gravity and Osric will not close the housing until it sits flat. He winds the tension on, notch by notch, and the slit narrows to a finger's width. Outside the port the tender is turning and the light off its hull moves across the bench. He fires the shutter once against his palm and feels the curtain drag at the end of its travel.
text_nonnarrative: Exposure in a focal plane housing was set by the width of a travelling slit and not by the speed of the curtain across the frame. Tension on the roller governed that speed; the two adjustments were independent. Drag at the end of the travel meant a wider slit on one side of the frame, so uneven density across the image was a property of the mechanism rather than of the light.

text_narrative: There was a dyer's daughter who printed the shapes of ferns on cloth and washed them in the stream at the foot of the garden. The blue held. When a hard winter came she washed in still water from the butt instead, and the ferns bled at every edge until the cloth was one flat colour. The old women told her the stream had wanted paying, and she carried a coin down to it in spring.
text_nonnarrative: Bleeding at the edge and a general loss of blue are two faults, and only the first is a fault of the washing itself. Bleeding is a matter of unreduced salt remaining in the cloth; loss of blue is a matter of water too weak in acid for the ferns to hold. A third case, in which the whole ground is flat and the shapes are even in tone with it, belongs to neither class.

text_narrative: A collector in the eastern counties reports that four prints from one album now carry a blue metallic sheen along their upper edges, and that the other eleven do not. The four sat in the same corner of the same box. A conservator engaged by the collector finds no difference in paper stock or in mount. The album's binder cannot be traced and the shop that supplied the board no longer trades under that name.
text_nonnarrative: Mirroring at the edge of a sheet and mirroring across its whole face were held to be separate faults. The first was a fault of storage and depended on air at the margins of a stack; the second was a fault of the fixing bath and was alike in every print of a batch. Blue sheen without either pattern was a third kind, attributed to the mount board rather than to the paper.

text_narrative: Four negatives came off the rack that August and Bettany lost the edge of three. The first frilled a quarter inch all round in a bath she had let go warm. On the second she chilled the water and the gelatin held everywhere but the notch. The third lifted in one sheet and slid off the glass entirely. The fourth she hardened first, and it dried down tight to the corners.
text_nonnarrative: Lifting is not frilling, though both leave gelatin off the glass. Frilling is confined to the margins and the centre is sound; lifting takes the film away in one sheet and has no preference for an edge. Between them sits a third condition, in which the emulsion stays whole but stands proud of the glass at the notch alone, and this is a fault of the hardening rather than of the bath.

text_narrative: The drawing table stands under the north light and the prism sits on its brass arm above the paper. Kestrel bends to the eyepiece and finds the room laid over the sheet, half sketch and half wall. The pencil point and the doorway share a place. She draws the doorway and the pencil goes on moving after her hand has stopped, out to the edge of the paper and off it.
text_nonnarrative: The near half of the drawing table is under the north light; the far half is in shadow all day. The prism stands on a brass arm at the table's upper edge, a hand's width above the paper and canted towards the window. Below the arm the sheet lies flat under two lead weights. The eyepiece is level with a seated head and the doorway is directly opposite it.

text_narrative: Everyone on the second survey used the coarse screen except the man who ground his own. He took a spare glass up to the ridge camp with a tin of emery and worked it in circles on a flat stone for two evenings. The grain came out finer than anything the outfitter sold, and in the flat light of the snowfields he could focus on a rope end at forty yards while the rest guessed.
text_nonnarrative: Above the last timber the ridge camp sits on a shelf of broken rock some two hundred paces long and half as wide. The snowfields are north of it and hold the light flat well into the evening. A grinding stone lies at the eastern end of the shelf, level enough for a glass, with the emery tins in a crevice behind. Water is forty yards down the slope and out of sight of the tents.

text_narrative: In the eleventh winter of the settlement the hall was still too short for the lantern. The keepers moved the machine back to the doorway and the picture filled the end wall for the first time, though the doorway would not then close. In the twelfth they cut a niche in the outer stone and set the lantern in that, and the picture held its size with the door shut.
text_nonnarrative: The hall was nine paces from the niche to the end wall, with the benches in four rows across the middle. The niche stood at head height in the outer stone, a foot deep and open to the hall on one side only. The end wall was plastered white from the floor to the roof beams and had no fitting of any kind. Doorway and niche were on the same axis.

text_narrative: The scale on the barrel said three feet to infinity at the smallest stop and Ilva did not believe a word of it. Whoever engraved it had never stood in a corridor at dusk with a sitter who would not keep still. Three feet was where the near figure went soft. She set the barrel two marks over what the scale allowed and made a note of it on the card.
text_nonnarrative: Engraved scales vary more between makers than between barrels from one maker. Across a sample of forty-one lenses the near limit marked at the smallest stop is optimistic by a median of eight inches, and in about a fifth of cases by more than a foot. Operators in institutional work allow for this by habit; among those surveyed, two thirds set the barrel short of the mark the scale gives.

text_narrative: A colony registrar confirms that the pigment charts hung in the dome corridor have gone unequal after nine years under the filtered sun. Reds at the western end are pale to the point of white. The registrar attributes the difference to hours of exposure rather than to the pigments, since the same reds at the eastern end hold their depth. A replacement set arrives on the next supply run.
text_nonnarrative: Fading varies more within a pigment class than between classes. Among lakes in common use, the spread from the fastest to the least fast is wider than the spread between lakes and earths taken as groups. Position accounts for most of the variation observed on hung charts: something near a third of the difference between two panels of the same colour is a matter of where each hangs.

text_narrative: When the sun-hall was raised the panels behind the throne were clear as water, and the makers laid on a resin they swore would never darken. Nine reigns passed. The gold in the panels went the colour of old honey and the blues beneath went green, and no light in the hall was to blame, for the shutters had been closed against it since the second reign.
text_nonnarrative: Yellowing was reported more often in closed halls than in lit ones, and the difference between the two groups was small beside the spread within either. Resin type accounted for the greater part of that spread. Among surveyed panels above eight reigns in age, near two thirds were described as honey or darker, and blues under a yellowed film were counted green in nine cases of ten.

text_narrative: There was a magpie who kept a tube of mirrors in her nest and would not be parted from it. Each bright thing she dropped in came back to her sixfold, and she counted the six as six and thought herself rich. A crow told her the angle of the glass made the number and not the world. She turned the tube until the angle changed, counted eight, and called the crow a liar.
text_nonnarrative: A kaleidoscope is a tube containing two or more mirrors set along its length at a fixed angle. The count of images is a function of that angle alone and is exact only where the angle divides evenly into a full turn. Angles that do not so divide give a broken figure at the seam. Object cell and eyehole have no bearing on the count, being matters of what is shown rather than of how often.

text_narrative: Saturdays are for the tinting box, and Merrow works through the family in order. The grandmother's cheeks take one pass of carmine and no more, because the print underneath is already warm. The uncle in uniform needs three passes and still looks bloodless. The baby she leaves alone. The last is a wedding group where the dresses go on soaking colour until the whole row of them is faintly pink and nobody notices.
text_nonnarrative: Hand tinting was the laying of transparent colour over a finished print, distinguished from painting by the fact that the image beneath remained the source of all tone. Its palette was therefore narrow, fixed by the print rather than by the colourist: pigments dense enough to hide the image were unusable, and warm papers restricted it further. Depth of colour was a matter of the number of passes, each pass being weak by design.

text_narrative: In the third spring of the requisition the studio was ordered to supply portraits for the register at four a day. The retoucher had one pencil and a bottle of medium and worked the negatives on a slanted glass by the window. Two hundred and nine plates went out that season. In the fourth spring the medium ran short and the pencil would not take, and the register accepted plain prints.
text_nonnarrative: Graphite retouching was work done on the negative rather than on the print, and was defined by that alone. Its medium was a varnish laid over the emulsion to give the pencil a tooth; without it the graphite had nothing at all to hold to. Density added to a negative was density taken from the print, so the whole craft was one of lightening the finished image and never of darkening it.

text_narrative: They still talk about the pair of cameras Ottway rigs on the finish rail. Most people set the two lenses a head's width apart and get a picture with some roundness in it. Ottway sets his at four feet and the runners come out like cut cardboard, one behind another, flat as a stack of plates. Nobody uses it for the judging but everybody queues to look at it afterwards.
text_nonnarrative: Separation between the two lenses was to be a head's width, and any greater figure required the sanction of the meeting. Mounts wider than a foot were permitted at the finish rail alone and were not to be shown in the general room. Both lenses were required to be of one focal length. Nothing in the rule bore on the height of the pair above the rail.

text_narrative: In the years when the town still owed its shadows to the hill, every house kept a printing frame on the roof and laid its dead year in it at midsummer. A sheet of paper under glass, a leaf or a ribbon on top, and the sun did the rest by noon. What came down was brown and exact. The hill took the shapes it was given and gave back the year without them.
text_nonnarrative: Glass in a printing frame is to be free of bubble and of visible tint. Backs hinged in two leaves are permitted where the paper is to be lifted at one corner for inspection; solid backs are required elsewhere. Pressure is to be even across the whole area, and a frame that bears only on its margins is not to be used for a leaf or for any other object of thickness.

text_narrative: The crack pattern on the small panel had not been there in the spring, Ossian was almost sure of it. Almost. A web that fine took forty years to open and this one had opened in six months, and the lines ran in a spiral, which no ground did. He held the lamp closer. The spiral tightened towards the sitter's left eye and stopped a finger's width short of it.
text_nonnarrative: Craquelure was always the least reliable evidence of age, and the reason was simple: the pattern belonged to the ground and not to the years. A panel prepared thin and dried fast could show a web within a decade, while a thick oil ground on canvas might stay whole for a century. Connoisseurs who read the pattern for a date were not wrong to read it, only wrong about what it recorded.

text_narrative: The streetlight sat just outside the frame and Devane could not get rid of it. Every plate came back with a chain of pale hexagons across the woman's coat, one for each surface in the barrel. He shifted the tripod a yard along the kerb and the chain swung the other way. In the end he shot from inside the doorway, with the lamp behind brick, and the coat came out black and clean.
text_nonnarrative: Flare is commonly treated as a defect of the lens, and this is half true at best. Each air-glass surface reflects a little, and a barrel of many elements has many such surfaces, so the fault is structural rather than one of workmanship. The remedy lies with the light and not with the glass: a source outside the frame but within the angle of the barrel is the whole of the trouble.

text_narrative: A projection house in the river district withdrew a print after two showings when the picture began to jump at every reel change. The house engineer measured the perforations and found the pitch short by a hundredth over four feet. The print had been stored for eleven years in a cellar with no record of its humidity. The distributor listed the copy as struck in the same month as three others that ran clean.
text_nonnarrative: Pitch: the distance from one perforation to the one following, measured along the same edge of the film. Short pitch: any pitch below the nominal figure, whether from shrinkage or from the original punch. Cumulative error: the sum of such differences over a stated length, conventionally four feet of film. Jump: the visible displacement of the picture where the pitch of the print and the pitch of the machine were unequal at the gate.

text_narrative: A stonecutter's apprentice was set to grain a slab for the sorcerer's press and told to stop when the surface would hold a breath. She ground it with sand and a muller for a day and a night. At dawn the stone showed a tooth like fine sugar, and she breathed on it, and the mark stayed. The sorcerer looked once and said she had gone a half day too far.
text_nonnarrative: Tooth: the fineness of the grained surface of a lithographic stone, expressed by the grade of sand last used upon it. Muller: the hand tool by which that sand is worked, distinct from the mechanical graining bed. Flat stone: any surface with too little tooth to hold a greasy mark. Sugar tooth: the finest grade in ordinary use. Over-graining: tooth so fine that the mark spreads into the grain and loses its edge.

text_narrative: In the fifth year after the Cantonal Accord the guild of platemakers was granted the sole right to buff. The register for that year lists eleven workshops in the capital and two beyond the wall. The buffing leather was to come from one tannery only, and a shipment of forty hides was recorded in the autumn. By the eighth year the count of workshops stood at three and the leather clause was struck out.
text_nonnarrative: Buffing means the working of a plate surface with leather and a dry powder, and does not include any operation employing a liquid. Where a plate is worked in both ways on one occasion, only the dry stage falls under this part. A workshop holding the right to buff is not thereby entitled to grain. Nothing in this part affects the standing of leather obtained outside the chartered tannery, nor the sale of powder.

text_narrative: Five boxes of resin came to the workshop that year and the master dusted a plate from each. The first gave a grain so coarse the bite ran between the grains and flooded. The second and third she could not tell apart. The fourth was fine enough for a sky and she used it all before autumn. The fifth had been stored damp, and it sat on the plate in cakes and would not melt at all.
text_nonnarrative: Aquatint grain means a resinous deposit fused to a plate in discrete particles, each particle standing as a resist in its own right and separate from its neighbours. A deposit fused into a continuous film is not a grain within this meaning, whatever its origin. Where particles of more than one size are present, the coarsest governs the classification. Nothing in this definition bears on the depth of the bite or on the number of stoppings.

text_narrative: In the first age the makers believed a smaller hole would always give a sharper world, and they pierced their shutters with needles and then with hairs. The pictures on the far wall grew soft again and no one could say why. It was the last of them, working with a hole no wider than a thought, who found the wall filled with a grey haze and named the limit that bears no maker's name.
text_nonnarrative: A hole counts as pierced only where a single instrument makes it in one entry of the material and one withdrawal. Two entries at one place yield no hole and the plate stands unpierced. A plate with more holes than one is out of the contest whatever its picture, and cannot be answered by covering the extra. No maker may set the wall at a distance shorter than the width of the frame itself.

text_narrative: Everyone in the house knows not to let the youngest near the splicer, and the reason is the lap. She scrapes the emulsion off in a hurry, lays the two ends over each other by half a frame, and floods the joint with cement until it squeezes out at the edges. The splice holds for one showing. On the second it opens at the sprocket and takes three frames with it.
text_nonnarrative: An overlap of less than a full frame is not a splice and has no standing in the reel. Emulsion remaining anywhere under the lap disqualifies the joint, however sound the joint appears. Cement outside the lap is a blemish and not a fault. A reel in which any joint crosses a sprocket hole is unfit for the machine, and the count of good joints elsewhere does not redeem it.

text_narrative: Nineteen boxes on the shelf and only one of them opened, which is not how Sennet left the darkroom. The fast plates are gone from the middle rank. Somebody has been working here at night and using the quickest stock, and the wet marks on the bench are cold. Not a burglar, then, since nothing of value is missing. Only speed. Only the boxes that would hold an image in one second.
text_nonnarrative: Nineteen boxes make up the shelf stock, in three speeds and two plate sizes. The slow rank holds nine, ordinary blue-sensitive plates, thick in the emulsion and good for a copy of a drawing. The middle rank runs to six and is the general studio plate in both sizes. Fast stock amounts to four boxes only, thin-coated and dated at six months, and these are kept apart at the darker end of the shelf.

text_narrative: Rain on the tin roof and the light going, and Odrin racks the bellows out to twice the focal length to fill the frame with a seed head. The image on the glass goes dim by two stops the moment the front standard passes the mark. He counts it off on the scale glued to the bed. Four seconds becomes sixteen. The seed head is dry and it does not move, which is the only luck in it.
text_nonnarrative: Four extension scales were glued to the bed of the camera, one for each of the lenses in the outfit. Each was a strip of paper marked in factors rather than in inches, the shortest running from one to four and the longest from one to sixteen. Two were printed and two were written by hand. All four were flush with the near rail and legible from the focusing cloth, and the hand-written pair were the ones in daily use.

text_narrative: A studio on the harbour road issues a corrected set of prints after buyers complain of dark corners in eleven of a run of forty. The studio attributes the darkening to a hood fitted for a longer lens than the one in use. The corrected set is printed from the same negatives with the corners burned less. No refund is offered and the original prints are not called in.
text_nonnarrative: Deliberate corner darkening was the laziest device in portrait work of the period. It was defended as a way of holding the eye on the face, but a face that needed a dark border to hold the eye was a face badly lit to begin with. The better studios used it once in a run of forty and were the ones whose prints still read as photographs rather than as lockets.

text_narrative: There was an engraver in a hill town who would not stipple, and said the dot was a coward's line. He cut everything in swelling strokes, faces and cloth and cloud alike, and his skies came out like water. One winter a plate he had cut in lines began to show dots where no dots were, a few each morning, until the sky above the town in it was grey with them.
text_nonnarrative: Pure line engraving was overrated by its own practitioners, who mistook difficulty for merit. Stipple did in one operation what the swelling stroke did in three, and did it more evenly in flesh, where evenness was the whole point. What the line school had over the stipplers was skies, and only skies. The best plates of the century were the ones that used both and made no announcement of it.

text_narrative: In the year the optical works took its second charter the shop had four formulae on the books and none of them held the corners. The computer engaged that spring worked through the winter on a symmetrical arrangement of six glasses in four groups. By the following charter year the corner definition matched the centre at every stop above the third, and the older formulae were withdrawn from the list.
text_nonnarrative: Whether flatness of field was one property of a lens or two was never settled in the trade. On one account a flat field and a corrected corner were the same thing described from different ends, since a curved field showed itself only as corner softness. On the other they were independent, and a lens could be flat and still bad at the margin. The dispute rested on what counted as definition.

text_narrative: Long before the fleets, the first watchers of the outer dark ground their lenses from a single kind of glass and saw every star wearing a violet skin. They took the skin for a property of stars. Generations held to it. Then a lens of two glasses came out of a shop on the third moon, and the skin was gone, and the stars were only points, and the watchers had to give the colour a new owner.
text_nonnarrative: Colour at the edge of an image belongs either to the thing or to the instrument, and nothing in the appearance itself decides which. A violet rim is an argument for the instrument only once a second instrument without the rim is available for comparison. Short of that, the two readings are equally good, and calling the rim a defect is a commitment rather than an observation. Fringing is thus a relational concept and not a simple one.

text_narrative: There was a printer in a mill town who copied a picture that had already been screened once, and set his own screen square with the first. The pattern that came up was not in the picture and not in either screen. It was a set of dark rings, and they were wider on the sheets he pulled after dark. He turned his screen thirty degrees and the rings went, and he never worked square again.
text_nonnarrative: The spacing of the beat pattern was inversely proportional to the angular difference between two screens of equal ruling. At a difference of one degree the beat was of the order of sixty times the screen pitch; at thirty degrees it was smaller than the pitch itself and invisible. The relation held only for equal rulings. Where the rulings differed, spacing depended on the difference in ruling as well as on the angle.

text_narrative: Three lamps on the crossing and the purser lights a different one each evening for the saloon show. The lime cylinder gives a steady white and eats a quarter inch an hour, which he can measure with a thumbnail. The arc is brighter and hisses and needs winding twice a reel. On the last night both fail in a swell and he shows the pictures by an oil flame, small and brown, and nobody leaves.
text_nonnarrative: Luminous output of a lime cylinder varied with the square of the gas pressure at the jet, up to the pressure at which the surface pits. Above that point the relation failed and output was governed instead by the rate of wear. An arc of equal candle power drew some forty times the current of the blower and was accordingly reserved for halls above a stated seating, whatever the price of the lime.

text_narrative: The panel is dry through and Ainsley knows the crack will not close, whatever the sign painter says about damp cloths. Eight coats of gesso on green pine, laid on in a week in July on a porch with the sun full on it. What did anyone expect. She runs a thumbnail down the line and a flake the size of a fingernail comes away in the dust of the yard.
text_nonnarrative: Below the paint film lay the ground, and below the ground the panel, three layers bonded and each with a different appetite for water. The ground itself was not one layer but eight or more, every coat thin and every one keyed to the coat beneath. Its outermost coats were the finest in grain. A sizing skin sat between the lowest coat and the wood, absent in cheaper work.

text_narrative: The survey party carried a painted panorama for the winter quarters, and by the third season the canvas would not hold its own weight. The carpenter glued a second cloth to the back of it with flour paste and a warm iron, working out from the middle. It went on the wall again and stayed flat for two more winters, though the join showed as a ridge across the sky.
text_nonnarrative: A relined picture has two fabrics where it had one, the original and a lining cloth of coarser weave behind it. Between them lies an adhesive layer, continuous in a good job and patchy in a poor one. The tacking margins of the original are usually absent, having no function once the lining takes the strain. Stretcher and keys are common to both states and are no part of the difference.
